explain.say: Have you ever asked why, and then why again? Long ago in Greece, some people made asking why their life's work. The board shows a timeline of these thinkers, from Socrates to Eratosthenes. Let's meet a few.

explain.say: Look at Socrates. He wrote nothing down. He walked around Athens asking people questions like, what is fairness? Then he asked more, until they really had to think. We still call this the Socratic method. Want to try it on a friend?

explain.say: See Hippocrates? Many people then thought illness was a punishment from the gods. Hippocrates said: look for natural causes, like food, water and air, and watch the patient carefully. Why is careful watching useful for a doctor?

explain.say: Jump to Euclid in Alexandria, in Egypt. Around 300 BCE he wrote the Elements, a book that builds geometry step by step from a few simple rules. It was used in schools for over 2,000 years! Which shapes do you already know?

explain.say: Last, Eratosthenes measured shadows in two Egyptian cities and worked out the size of the whole Earth, remarkably close to the real answer. Great job, young thinker! Wow: he did it with a stick, sunlight and maths, about 2,260 years ago.

faq.a: It is a way of learning by asking questions. Socrates asked someone what they believed, then asked more questions to test it, helping them think more clearly.
A Greek doctor from the island of Kos, born around 460 BCE. He taught that diseases have natural causes, and the Hippocratic Oath for doctors is named after him.
asks: Who is the father of medicine?

faq.a: Almost everything: logic, animals, plants, politics, poetry and the stars. He was taught by Plato and later taught the young Alexander the Great.
A set of 13 books of geometry and numbers written around 300 BCE in Alexandria. It proves ideas step by step and was a school textbook for over 2,000 years.
Archimedes of Syracuse explained how levers work and why objects float, and found a very good value for pi. Legend says he shouted Eureka, I have found it, in his bath.

facts: Euclid's Elements, written around 300 BCE, has 13 books.
Eratosthenes estimated Earth's circumference around 240 BCE using shadows at Syene and Alexandria.

quiz.why: He questioned people so they would think more deeply.

wrong.1: Socrates wrote nothing; we know him through Plato and others.
wrong.2: He talked and questioned rather than setting tests.

quiz.say: Who worked out the size of the Earth using shadows?
quiz.show: Who measured the Earth with shadows?
quiz.why: Eratosthenes compared shadows in two Egyptian cities to estimate Earth's size.

wrong.1: Euclid wrote about geometry but did not measure the Earth.
